extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning introductory set theory and mathematical logic / readers of an introductory discrete mathematics or proofs textbook
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, notations, examples, and basic rules for set operations (union, intersection, difference, complement, indexed unions/intersections, Venn diagrams) and elementary propositional logic (statements, conjunction/disjunction/negation, conditionals). Intended to teach and exercise foundational skills for proof-writing and set/logic manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The union of A and B is the set A ∪ B = {x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In words, A ∪ B is the set of all things that are in A or in B (or in both). Examples: AuB = {a,b,c,d,e,f}. Property noted: X ∪ Y = Y ∪ X (commutative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The intersection of A and B is the set A ∩ B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In words, A ∩ B is the set of all things in both A and B. Examples: A ∩ B = {d,e}. Property noted: X ∩ Y = Y ∩ X (commutative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference of A and B is the set A - B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∉ B}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In words, A - B is the set of all things that are in A but not in B. Examples: A - B = {a,b,c}. Note: in general X - Y ≠ Y - X.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complement definition (with universal set)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a set with universal set U, the complement of A, denoted A^c (or A with bar), is A^c = U - A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The universal set U is the ambient set in context (e.g., N for primes). Example: If P is primes, then P^c = N - P = {1,4,6,8,...}. When unspecified, the universal set is often denoted U.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartesian product examples and interaction with set operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Cartesian product A×B combines two sets into ordered pairs (x,y). Examples show how product interacts with union/intersection: (A×C) ∩ (B×C) = (A∩B)×C and (A∩B)×B enumerated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate products of graphs (sets of pairs) and how operations on factors affect the product (e.g., (A×C) ∩ (B×C) = (A∩B)×C). Used to visualize set operations in R^2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venn diagram usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent sets by circles/ovals to visualize unions, intersections, and differences; useful as informal 'scratch work' to understand combinations of sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples shown for two and three sets; shading conventions illustrated; used to deduce equalities/inequalities between set expressions and to help plan proofs or problem-solving strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses rules for expressions with ∪ and ∩ (Important Points)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an expression involving sets uses only ∪, parentheses are optional; if it uses only ∩, parentheses are optional; if an expression uses both ∪ and ∩, parentheses are essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from associativity of ∪ and ∩ (e.g., (A∪B)∪C = A∪(B∪C)), but mixed operations are not generally associative/commutative with each other, so placement of parentheses matters. Venn diagrams illustrate differences like (A∪B)∩C versus A∪(B∩C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexed unions and intersections notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Given sets A1,A2,...,An (or A_i for i in some index set), define ⋃_{i=1}^n A_i = A1 ∪ A2 ∪ ... ∪ An and ⋂_{i=1}^n A_i = A1 ∩ A2 ∩ ... ∩ An; this extends to infinite lists using ⋃_{i=1}^∞ and ⋂_{i=1}^∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notation analogous to sigma notation for sums; definitions: ⋃_{i=1}^∞ A_i = {x : x ∈ A_i for at least one i}, ⋂_{i=1}^∞ A_i = {x : x ∈ A_i for every i}. Examples given (finite and infinite) and how to interpret them geometrically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexed collections with arbitrary index sets
rubrics_metrics.description: If a family {A_a : a ∈ J} is given, ⋃_{a∈J} A_a = {x : x ∈ A_a for at least one a∈J} and ⋂_{a∈J} A_a = {x : x ∈ A_a for every a∈J}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index set J need not be integers; it can be any set (e.g., real interval [0,2]). Examples show unions over [0,2] producing a 2-D region from 1-D slices: ⋃_{a∈[0,2]} [1,2]×{a} = [1,2]×[0,2].

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of set notation and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful mapping between set-builder expressions and geometric/elementwise descriptions (e.g., AuB = {(x,y) : y = x^2 or y = x+2} for graphs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show how to write unions/intersections/differences of graph-sets in set-builder notation and how to remove points (holes) using differences: A - B = {(x,x^2) : x ∈ R - {-1,2}}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement (proposition) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement is a sentence or mathematical expression that is either definitely true or definitely false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish statements from non-statements (commands/questions) and from open sentences whose truth depends on variables. Use letters P,Q,R to denote statements; P(x) denotes a sentence about variable x, which may be open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open sentences and variables in statements
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence containing variables (e.g., Q(x): 'x is even') is an open sentence and is not a statement unless the variables are specified or quantified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use P(x), P(x,y) notation to indicate dependence on variables. Open sentences become statements when quantifiers or particular values are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: correct logic vs correct information
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic is a process of deducing information correctly, not just deducing correct information; valid logical inference can produce a (logically) correct conclusion even when premises are false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: deducing area from radius—if premises are incorrect the logic can still be valid. Emphasizes importance of separating validity of argument from truth of premises when proving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjunction (and) truth table and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: If P and Q are statements, P ∧ Q denotes 'P and Q' and is true exactly when both P and Q are true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth table provided. Use ∧ to combine statements asserting both conditions hold. Examples of true/false combinations given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disjunction (or) truth table and inclusive meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: If P and Q are statements, P ∨ Q denotes 'P or Q' and is true when at least one of P or Q is true (inclusive or).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth table provided; mathematical 'or' is inclusive (true when both true). To express exclusive 'or' or 'but not both', explicitly say so (e.g., 'P or Q, but not both' or 'Either P or Q'). Examples illustrate everyday vs mathematical usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation (not) truth table
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a statement P, ¬P means 'It is not true that P' and is true exactly when P is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth table with two lines. Several equivalent phrasings for negation illustrated (e.g., 'The number 2 is not even').

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional (if...then) statements and truth table
rubrics_metrics.description: For statements P and Q, P ⇒ Q (or 'If P then Q') is the conditional which is false only when P is true and Q is false; otherwise it is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth table provided. Many equivalent phrasings listed (Q if P; Q whenever P; P is sufficient for Q; Q is necessary for P; P only if Q). Example: 'If you pass the exam, then you will pass the course' analyzed across four scenarios to illustrate truth conditions (antecedent false cases make the conditional true).
